It was past one in the hostel, and the corridor lights had gone to their night setting. In room 214, Disha sat cross-legged on her bed with her thumb over the message box. "Are you awake?" was already typed to Kabir. She had ended it three weeks ago.

Her roommate Mehak looked up from her notes. "Disha."

"I know." Disha's voice was small. "I just want to see if he still replies."

"And if he does?"

Disha stared at the words. She wanted a reply so badly she could taste it, and she knew it would not answer anything she was really asking. She deleted the message, muted his chat, and pushed the phone into her desk drawer.

"Also," she said, "I'm not asking Riya to check what he's up to. That's not fair on anyone."

Mehak slid over her packet of biscuits. Neither of them said anything for a while.

qa.q: What time was it in the hostel when Disha typed the message?
qa.a: It was past one in the hostel.

qa.q: What did Disha want from the message, and what did she realise about it?
qa.a: She wanted to see if Kabir still replied, and she realised a reply would not answer what she was really asking.

qa.q: What steps did Disha take, and what else might help over the next few weeks?
qa.a: She deleted the message, muted his chat and put her phone away, and she could keep leaning on friends like Mehak while time does its work.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Disha's night-time struggle?
qa.a: Mehak probably sees a roommate in pain who is trying to do the right thing, and offers quiet company instead of advice.

grounding: Shows the urge to text an ex at night, resolved by a conscious choice to mute and not test whether they still care or use friends to keep tabs.

The monsoon had knocked the power out across the colony, and the last bus was cancelled. Sumit stood at Mridul's door with a wet book bag. "Sorry, I only came to return your jacket. Can I wait it out?"

Mridul lit a candle and made chai on the gas. They had been "friends" for two months, and he had told himself it was going fine. Yet his pulse jumped when Sumit laughed.

They talked easily until Sumit mentioned a girl he'd met at a workshop, smiling into the candlelight. Mridul kept his face still and felt his stomach sink.

When the rain slowed, he walked Sumit to the gate. "I think I need some space," he said. "Being friends right now is harder for me than I thought. I'd like to try again later, maybe."

Sumit nodded, quietly. "I'm sorry. I get it."

qa.q: Why had Sumit come to Mridul's door on that stormy evening?
qa.a: He came to return Mridul's jacket, and then had to wait out the storm because the last bus was cancelled.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when Sumit spoke about a girl from a workshop?
qa.a: His stomach sank; he still hoped, so hearing about someone new hurt while he kept his face still.

qa.q: What did Mridul do that showed honesty about the friendship, and why is distance a good first step?
qa.a: He told Sumit the friendship was harder than he expected and asked for space, which stops him staying close just to keep a door open.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Mridul asked for space?
qa.a: Sumit may have felt sorry and a little surprised, but he understood, so he respected the request without arguing.

grounding: Shows attempted friendship after a breakup while one still hopes, with honest recognition that it hurts and a request for distance.

passage:
For weeks Kavitha replayed it: how Vinod had said he was at his cousin's when he was at the movies with someone else, how her mother's neighbours had heard first. Every time the scene ran in her head, her jaw got tighter.

At the sewing shop in the bazaar, her friend Ayesha was threading a machine. "You're grinding your teeth again," Ayesha said.

Kavitha nearly blurted out what she knew about Vinod's father's debts. The words were right there, sharp and satisfying.

She held them back. "I'm furious," she said instead. "He lied to me, and I let him. That's why I'm angry, and it's fair."

Ayesha nodded and kept quiet. Kavitha felt some of the heat leave her chest.

That evening on the terrace she said to herself: enough for today. She went down to help with dinner.

qa.q: Where did Vinod say he was when he was really at the movies with someone else?
qa.a: He said he was at his cousin's.

qa.q: What was Kavitha about to do when she nearly blurted out something about Vinod's father, and why did she hold back?
qa.a: She was tempted to hurt him by telling something private, but held back because it was not hers to spread and would not give her peace.

qa.q: How did Kavitha handle her anger in the sewing shop, and what else could she do?
qa.a: She said plainly that she was furious and why, without exposing Vinod's private matters; she could keep letting the anger go bit by bit, for her own peace.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have seen Kavitha's outburst being held back?
qa.a: Ayesha is likely to feel trusted and relieved that her friend is not turning the shop against Vinod, and she can simply listen.

grounding: Shows replaying a wrong and feeling bitter, with anger named and let go while a private matter is not spread.

passage:
I'm Rehana, Jyoti's classmate, and I'm writing down what I saw because she asked me to.

For about two weeks I noticed her checking her phone all the time. Her ex, Amit, kept messaging and once waited outside the college gate. I can't know exactly how Jyoti felt, but she looked shaky, and she stopped eating lunch in the canteen.

One afternoon she told him once, calmly and clearly, that it was over and that he must stop. Then she blocked him. Messages arrived from other numbers, so she took screenshots of them and saved each one.

I went with her to the warden, and she rang her elder brother that night. Jyoti kept saying, "Maybe I made it worse." I told her none of this was her fault. It isn't.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do with the messages that came from other numbers?
qa.a: She took screenshots of them and saved each one.

qa.q: What does Rehana's account suggest about how Jyoti was feeling, and how sure can she be?
qa.a: Jyoti looked shaky and stopped eating lunch in the canteen and said 'Maybe I made it worse', so she seems frightened and self-blaming, though Rehana admits she cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that was wise, and what should she keep doing?
qa.a: She said one clear final no, blocked him, saved evidence and told the warden and her brother; she should keep telling trusted people if the contact continues.

qa.q: How might Amit see the moment when Jyoti told him it was over?
qa.a: He may feel rejected and refuse to accept it, but her clear no means the decision was not open to negotiation.

grounding: Shows an ex who keeps contacting after a no, with a clear final refusal, blocking, saved evidence and telling trusted people.

passage:
It was eleven at night and Akash's chemistry exam was at nine the next morning. His textbook lay open on the desk, unread. On his phone he was refreshing Jahnavi's profile for the fortieth time, looking at a photo of her at a friend's birthday, counting who stood beside her.

A power cut plunged the room into darkness and left only the glow of his screen. Somehow that made it worse. He felt a hollow, wild ache in his chest, and he could not stop.

He remembered his cousin's voice: "That's not love, that's pain looking for something to hold." Akash put the phone face down.

In the morning, after the exam, he walked to the college counselling room and sat down in the waiting chair. When his name was called, he said, "I can't stop watching her life. I need help."

His hands were shaking, but he stayed.

qa.q: How many times had Akash refreshed Jahnavi's profile by the time the power cut came?
qa.a: He was refreshing it for the fortieth time.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he stared at Jahnavi's photo and could not stop?
qa.a: A hollow, wild ache, meaning hurt and a sense of being stuck instead of clear love.

qa.q: What did Akash do that was a good step, and why?
qa.a: He put the phone down and went to the counselling room to ask for help, because obsessively watching her only kept the pain fresh.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see it if Akash kept monitoring her and later showed up?
qa.a: She could feel watched and unsafe, and her life would be shaped by his hurt instead of her own choices.

grounding: Shows being unable to stop watching an ex's life, recognised as pain rather than love, with support sought from a counsellor.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Eshaan came in without an appointment and sat at the very edge of the chair. He said his ex, Mridul, still has private pictures and messages from when they were together, and since the breakup Eshaan has been afraid Mridul might share them. No threat has been made, but he can't sleep or concentrate, and he said, "I feel so stupid and ashamed."

I told him that private material being shared without consent is a crime, and that the shame belongs to the person who misuses it, not to him. He looked up at that.

We agreed he'd keep any messages as they are, not delete them, and I helped him plan to speak with his elder cousin tonight. We also talked about how to reach the cyber cell if it ever comes to that. He left looking less alone.

qa.q: What is Eshaan afraid that Mridul might do?
qa.a: He is afraid Mridul might share the private pictures and messages.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he said he felt stupid and ashamed?
qa.a: Fear and shame, together with poor sleep and trouble concentrating, since he worries about the material being leaked.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest Eshaan do, and why?
qa.a: Keep the messages as they are, talk to his elder cousin, and know how to reach the cyber cell, because he should not carry this alone and it is a crime, not his shame.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel after the counsellor said the shame belongs to whoever misuses the material?
qa.a: He might feel a weight lifted, since he sees he is not the one at fault, and feel less alone in facing it.

grounding: Shows fear of an ex leaking private material, met with the reminder that it is a crime not shame, keeping evidence, and telling a trusted adult or the cyber cell.

passage:
Rekha's father found out that she had been seeing someone, and that it had ended, on the same evening, through a neighbour. At dinner in the village house, no one said much. Her mother sighed at the dal. Her father said, "What will people say?"

Rekha felt her ears burn, and for a moment the old reflex rose: say it was nothing, that there had never been anyone. She stopped herself. A deeper lie would only make the house colder.

After dinner she went to the roof, where her cousin Charu was sitting with a lamp and a shawl. "Didi, they think I've brought disgrace."

Charu shifted over. "Did you do anything wrong by loving someone and then ending it?"

The next morning Rekha told her mother, "It ended. I'm sad. I'll tell you more when I'm ready." Her mother didn't answer, but she put a hand on Rekha's hair.

qa.q: How did Rekha's father learn about her romance and its ending?
qa.a: He found out through a neighbour.

qa.q: What did Rekha feel like doing when her father asked what people would say, and why did she not do it?
qa.a: She felt like saying there had never been anyone, but she stopped because a deeper lie would only make the house colder.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that helped her stay honest without saying everything?
qa.a: She found Charu for compassion and then told her mother it ended and she would say more when ready, choosing what to share.

qa.q: How might Rekha's mother feel about her daughter's answer the next morning?
qa.a: She may feel worried and unsure but softened by her daughter's honesty, which her hand on Rekha's hair suggests.

grounding: Shows parents judging after they learn of a relationship and its end, with the person seeking compassion, sharing only what she chooses and avoiding deeper lies.

Teacher's note, farewell tea, Saturday. I was handing out plates at the door when Kalyani and Ritu met face to face; I knew they had been together before. Ritu had arrived a few minutes after Kalyani.

Both paused. Kalyani's shoulders rose slightly, then dropped. She said, "Hi, Ritu. Good to see you," in an ordinary voice. Ritu said hello back. Kalyani added, "I'm going to say hello to Neha," and walked over to the snacks, and that was all.

She didn't put on a big laugh or a show of being fine, and neither of them made a remark about the other. Later I saw her talking with two classmates and eating a samosa, calmer than I had expected.

I said nothing to either of them afterwards. It seemed better to let it stay as brief as they had made it.

qa.q: Who did Kalyani go to greet after meeting Ritu?
qa.a: She went to say hello to Neha.

qa.q: What does it suggest about Kalyani that her shoulders rose and then dropped?
qa.a: It suggests a moment of tension that she managed, so she could stay polite and steady instead of reacting.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that made the meeting go smoothly?
qa.a: She was polite and brief, without a show of happiness or a sharp remark, and moved on to greet someone else.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Kalyani's short, ordinary greeting?
qa.a: Ritu may feel relieved that there was no scene, and may also feel a small pang that it was so brief.

grounding: Shows meeting an ex by chance at a gathering and handling it politely, briefly and calmly, without a scene or a show.

Last week I walked past the bookshop where Nilesh and I used to spend Sundays, and I felt a small, warm ache instead of a stab. "Gurleen, you're smiling at a shelf," my friend said. I was.

Months ago I couldn't have done that. Now I can look back at it without hurt. Some of it was good: he taught me how to make rajma, and he was kind to my grandmother. Some of it wasn't. I noticed I go quiet when something bothers me and hope the other person guesses, then feel invisible when they don't. I need someone who answers plainly, and I need to ask plainly, too.

I used to think I'd never trust anyone again. That has faded. It wasn't all bad and it wasn't all wonderful; it was real, and it's over. I'm open to love again, slowly.

qa.q: What did Nilesh teach Gurleen to make?
qa.a: He taught her how to make rajma.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's small warm ache, instead of a stab, suggest about how she now feels toward Nilesh?
qa.a: Some fondness remains, but the hurt has faded; she can remember the good, such as the rajma, and the lessons, like going quiet when bothered, without pain.

qa.q: What is Gurleen doing well in the way she looks back, and what could she try next?
qa.a: She holds the good and the bad honestly, without calling it all bad or all good, and she could practise asking plainly when something bothers her.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's friend see the change in her?
qa.a: Her friend sees her smiling at a shelf near the old bookshop, which suggests she seems lighter and more at peace than in earlier months.

grounding: Shows acceptance months after a breakup, with lessons about her patterns and needs, a balanced view of the past, and openness to love again.

passage:
I'm Shreya, and I sit behind Chetan in Economics. I noticed something small last Thursday and it's stayed with me.

Chetan and Leela were on the bench outside the canteen, talking about a film. I saw him turn toward her and say, "Can I hold your hand?" She looked at her lap for a second. Then she said, "Not right now."

I thought he might look hurt or push. Instead, he said, "Okay. Thanks for telling me," and leaned back a little, and they kept talking as before. I can't know what he felt inside; his knee was bouncing.

A few minutes later, Leela slid her hand across the bench, palm up. He looked at it for a moment, then took it gently.

It wasn't dramatic, but I remember thinking that asking and listening looks pretty simple.

qa.q: Where were Chetan and Leela sitting when he asked to hold her hand?
qa.a: They were on the bench outside the canteen.

qa.q: What might Chetan have been feeling after Leela said 'Not right now', and how sure is Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya cannot know for sure, but his bouncing knee suggests he may have felt a bit nervous or disappointed while he chose to accept the answer.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that made it safe for Leela to change her mind?
qa.a: He accepted the no with thanks and did not push, so she could decide later without pressure.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt when Chetan thanked her instead of pushing?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and safe, which may be why she offered her hand herself a few minutes later.

grounding: Shows wanting closeness by asking and listening, with a hesitation respected and later choice freely given.
